title: "Designing a Rule Set for a Simple Game"
description: "Seminar · Write the rules of a farm robot as conditions, make its decision table, put the rules in the right order, clean the conditions and test them at the border."
seminar: 7

No new ideas today: you apply what you learned in Lecture 12 to the rule set
of one simple game. Do each activity alone, then open "Check your result".
Every question on this page has its answer: try first, then check.

## Recall

- De Morgan: `!(p && q)` = `!p || !q`, and `!(p || q)` = `!p && !q`.
- Absorption `p || (p && q)` = `p`; complement `p && !p` = false.
- "But not both" is `^`; "unless p" means "if not p".
- A decision table has 2^n rows and one action in each row. In an else-if
  chain the first true rule wins.

::: {.callout-tip title="Try it 1 · Recall"}
Choose the right answer.

::: {.match extra="!p && !q|8"}
Which condition is the same as `!(p && q)`?
:   !p || !q

    Why: De Morgan: NOT each part, and && becomes ||.

How many rows has a decision table with 4 conditions?
:   16

    Why: 2^4 = 16.

Two rules of an else-if chain are true. Which one runs?
:   the first one from the top

    Why: the chain stops at the first true rule.
:::
:::

## Activity 1 · The rules in words become conditions

*Harvest Bot* is a small farm game: a robot works in a field. The designer
writes its rules in words. The facts are b (the battery is low), f (the
basket is full), p (a ripe crop is near), d (the soil is dry), r (it is
raining) and n (it is night).

![Rule words and their logic.](images/rule-words.png){width=90%}

::: {.callout-note title="Activity 1 · Words to conditions · 10 min"}
Write each rule as a C# condition with the letters.

1. The bot waters when the soil is dry and it is not raining.
2. The bot goes home when the battery is low or the basket is full.
3. The bot picks a crop when one is ripe, unless it is night.
4. "The bot does not water" is `!(d && !r)`. Write it without a NOT in
   front of the brackets.

*Your product:* four conditions.

::: {.check}
1. `d && !r`. 2. `b || f`. 3. `p && !n`: "unless n" is "if not n".
4. De Morgan: `!d || !!r`, so `!d || r`: the soil is not dry, or it rains.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Try it 2 · Rules to conditions"}
Harvest Bot: b battery low, f basket full, p ripe crop, d dry soil, r rain,
n night. Choose the condition.

::: {.match extra="p && n|d || !r"}
The bot waters when the soil is dry and it is not raining.
:   d && !r

    Why: "and" is &&, "not" is !.

The bot picks a crop when one is ripe, unless it is night.
:   p && !n

    Why: "unless n" means "if not n".

The bot does not water: !(d && !r).
:   !d || r

    Why: De Morgan, then !!r is r.
:::
:::

## Activity 2 · The decision table of the bot

The designer gives the order of the rules: "The bot goes home when the
battery is low (b). Otherwise it picks when a ripe crop is near (p).
Otherwise it waters when the soil is dry (d). Otherwise it waits."

![A decision table: every case, one action.](images/decision-table.png){width=86%}

::: {.callout-note title="Activity 2 · Make the table · 12 min"}
1. Make the table of b, p and d with all 8 rows and the action of each row.
2. In how many rows does the bot go home, pick, water and wait?
3. Is the table complete? Does a row have two actions?

*Your product:* an 8-row table, four counts and two answers.

::: {.check}
Home in the 4 rows with b = T. With b = F: Pick in 2 rows (p = T, d = T or
F); Water in 1 row (p = F, d = T); Wait in 1 row (p = F, d = F). 4 + 2 + 1 + 1
= 8. The table is complete (every row has an action) and has no conflict
(one action in each row).
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Try it 3 · The table"}
Harvest Bot: home if b; otherwise pick if p; otherwise water if d; otherwise
wait. Choose the action. You can use an answer more than once.

::: {.match extra="Water"}
b = F, p = T, d = T.
:   Pick

    Why: the battery is fine, and a ripe crop comes before the dry soil.

b = T, p = T, d = T.
:   Home

    Why: a low battery comes first, in every row.

b = F, p = F, d = F.
:   Wait

    Why: no rule is true, so the last action runs.

In how many of the 8 rows does the bot go home?
:   4

    Why: half of the rows have b = T.
:::
:::

## Activity 3 · Put the rules in order and clean them

A programmer writes the rules of the bot like this:

```csharp
if (p) Pick();
else if (b) Home();
else if (d && !b) Water();
else Wait();
```

![The same rules in a wrong and a right order.](images/rule-order.png){width=86%}

::: {.callout-note title="Activity 3 · Order and clean · 10 min"}
1. Test the row b = T, p = T, d = F. What does the chain do? What does the
   designer want?
2. Write the chain in the right order.
3. In your chain, `d && !b` can become `d`. Why?
4. Another rule says `if (!(!b && !f)) Home();`. Write it without a NOT in
   front of the brackets.

*Your product:* one bug, one chain, one reason and one condition.

::: {.check}
1. The chain picks, but the designer wants Home: the battery is low.
2. `if (b) Home(); else if (p) Pick(); else if (d) Water(); else Wait();`
3. The bot reaches the Water rule only when b is false, so `!b` is always
   true there, and `d && true` is `d` (identity).
4. De Morgan and double negation: `b || f`.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Try it 4 · Order and clean"}
Choose the right answer.

::: {.match extra="Pick()|b && f"}
The chain `if (p) Pick(); else if (b) Home(); …` with b = T, p = T. What runs?
:   Pick(), but the designer wants Home()

    Why: the first true rule wins, and Pick is first.

Which rule must come first in the bot's chain?
:   if (b) Home();

    Why: the designer says a low battery beats every other rule.

What is `!(!b && !f)` without a NOT in front of the brackets?
:   b || f

    Why: De Morgan: !!b || !!f, then double negation.
:::
:::

## Activity 4 · Test the rules at the border

The designer says: "The battery is low when it is **under 20 %**." The code
says `bool b = battery <= 20;`.

![Testing at the border of a rule.](images/edge-cases.png){width=86%}

::: {.callout-note title="Activity 4 · Edge cases · 12 min"}
1. Test battery = 10 and battery = 80. Do the rule and the code agree?
2. Which value of the battery finds the bug? Write the fix.
3. A new rule: "The bot sells the apples when it has **at least 50**
   apples and **fewer than 3** trips today." Write the condition and four
   edge-case tests (apples, trips) with the expected result.

*Your product:* one bug with its fix, one condition and four tests.

::: {.check}
1. Yes: 10 is low in both, 80 is not low in both. These tests find nothing.
2. Battery = 20: the rule says "not low", but the code says low. Fix:
   `battery < 20`. 3. `apples >= 50 && trips < 3`. Tests, for example:
   (50, 2) sell; (49, 2) no; (50, 3) no; (51, 2) sell.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Try it 5 · Edge cases"}
Choose the right answer.

::: {.match extra="10|apples > 50"}
The rule is battery < 20, the code is battery <= 20. Which test finds the bug?
:   battery = 20

    Why: only at the border do < and <= give different results.

"At least 50 apples". The condition?
:   apples >= 50

    Why: "at least 50" includes 50.

Sell when apples >= 50 && trips < 3. The test (50, 3)?
:   do not sell

    Why: 3 trips is not fewer than 3.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-note .ai-task title="Task with AI · The rule set of a boss"}
**Goal:** a complete rule set with four conditions: a 16-row decision table
and an else-if chain. That is long by hand; an AI assistant writes it, and
you check it.

1. **Do it yourself:** read the rules of the boss. "The boss heals when its
   health is under 25 (h) and it has a potion (q). Otherwise it raises its
   shield when the player charges (c). Otherwise it attacks when the player
   is near (n). Otherwise it walks."
2. **Ask the AI:** copy this prompt and add the rules.

   ::: {.prompt}
   Here are the rules of a game boss in words. Make the decision table with
   all 16 rows of the conditions h, q, c, n (the first column 8 T, then 8 F)
   and the action in each row. Count the rows of each action. Then write the
   rules as one C# else-if chain in the right order, and give three
   edge-case tests for "health under 25". Rules:
   :::

3. **Check:** are there exactly 16 different rows? Check three rows by hand.
   Is the order of the chain the order of the designer? Do the edge-case
   tests use 24, 25 and 26? Is the code `health < 25`, not `<= 25`?

*Your product:* the table, the chain, your three hand checks and one
sentence on a mistake you found (or "no mistake").

::: {.check}
Heal 4 rows (h and q true), Shield 6 rows, Attack 3 rows, Walk 3 rows:
4 + 6 + 3 + 3 = 16. The chain: `if (h && q) Heal(); else if (c) Shield();
else if (n) Attack(); else Walk();`. Tests: health 24 heals (with a potion),
25 and 26 do not. AI tools often put Shield first, write `<= 25`, or repeat
or forget a row: look for all three.
:::
:::

## Game challenge: The guard of Torch Hall {.challenge}

Work alone. Use every activity of today.

The guard of *Torch Hall* has three facts: s (it sees the player), n (the
player is near) and w (it is weak: health **under 30**). Its rules: a weak
guard flees; otherwise it attacks a player it sees near; otherwise it chases
a player it sees; otherwise it patrols. Now the designer adds a fourth fact,
a (the guard hears the alarm), and a new rule: "the guard runs to the bell
when it hears the alarm, **unless it is weak**. The alarm is more important
than the player."

{{< sim file="sims/guard-brain.html" poster="sims/guard-brain.png" title="Guard Brain: rules, order and the decision table" height="900" >}}

::: {.callout-tip title="Try it 6 · The new rule set (harder)"}
The guard: s sees, n near, w weak (health under 30), a hears the alarm.
Flee if w; the bell if a, unless w; the alarm beats the player; then Attack
(s and n), Chase (s), Patrol. Choose the right answer.

::: {.match extra="8|health = 29"}
How many rows has the new decision table?
:   16

    Why: four facts: 2^4 = 16.

Where does the bell rule go in the chain?
:   after Flee, before Attack

    Why: "unless it is weak" puts Flee above it; the alarm beats the player.

In how many of the 16 rows does the guard run to the bell?
:   4

    Why: w = F and a = T; s and n can be anything: 2 × 2.

Health 30, the guard sees the player near, no alarm. The action?
:   Attack

    Why: 30 is not under 30, so the guard is not weak.

The code says `health <= 30`. Which test finds the bug?
:   health = 30

    Why: the border: the rule says "not weak", the code says weak.
:::
:::

## Wrap-up {.summary}

- You can write the rules of a game in words as conditions.
- You can make the decision table of a rule set and check that it is complete.
- You can put the rules of an else-if chain in the right order and clean them.
- You can test a number rule at its border with edge cases.
